figures.headline: Data Interpreter splits a project into a task graph of subtasks, each expanded into an action graph of code actions.
citing_sentences: Drawing inspiration from the application of hierarchical planning in automated machine learning tasks (Mohr et al., 2018; Mubarak & Koeshidayatullah, 2023), we organize the data science workflow via hierarchical structure, which initially decomposes the intricate data science problem into manageable tasks and further break down each task into specific actions executed through code (see Figure 2).

As shown in Figure 2, an example workflow decomposed by Data Interpreter for a machine operational status prediction problem, might include tasks like:data exploration, correlation analysis, outliers detection, feature engineering, model training, model evaluation, and visualization.
As illustrated in Figure 2, the visualization task is divided into three distinct actions, with the confusion matrix calculation handled by sklearn.

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have shown effectiveness across many applications. However, their use in data science scenarios requiring solving long-term interconnected tasks, dynamic data adjustments and domain expertise remains challenging. Previous approaches primarily focus on individual tasks, making it difficult to assess the complete data science workflow. Moreover, they struggle to handle real-time changes in intermediate data and fail to adapt dynamically to evolving task dependencies inherent to data science problems. In this paper, we present Data Interpreter, an LLM-based agent designed to automatically solve various data science problems end-to-end. Our Data Interpreter incorporates two key modules: 1) Hierarchical Graph Modeling, which breaks down complex problems into manageable subproblems, enabling dynamic node generation and graph optimization; and 2) Programmable Node Generation, a technique that refines and verifies each subproblem to iteratively improve code generation results and robustness. Extensive experiments consistently demonstrate the superiority of Data Interpreter. On InfiAgent-DABench, it achieves a $25\%$ performance boost, raising accuracy from $75.9\%$ to $94.9\%$. For machine learning and open-ended tasks, it improves performance from $88\%$ to $95\%$, and from $60\%$ to $97\%$, respectively. Moreover, on the MATH dataset, Data Interpreter achieves remarkable performance with a $26\%$ improvement compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT.

sections.body: The introduction states that earlier LLM agents for data science focus on individual tasks and lack end-to-end evaluation. Data Interpreter represents a workflow as a hierarchical graph in which tasks are nodes and dependencies are edges, and the graph changes as data and requirements change. Its Programmable Node Generation component generates, refines and verifies each node. The authors report a 25% performance boost on InfiAgent-DABench and a 26% improvement on the MATH dataset over baselines. Figure 1 compares it with other open-source frameworks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Data Interpreter targets end-to-end data science workflows, which prior LLM agents handled only as isolated tasks.

sections.body: The related work groups prior work into three areas. LLM data science agents include code interpreters and a hyperparameter tuning method that handles single tasks rather than full pipelines. Tool-enhancement work covers retrieval and tool selection across multi-agent systems. Graph-based planning methods, including ToT, GoT and DSPy, refine prompts or pipeline structure but often struggle with the multi-step, task-dependent problems common in data science. The authors conclude that end-to-end frameworks for data science remain insufficiently developed.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior LLM data science agents cover individual tasks, so end-to-end graph-based frameworks for data science remain underdeveloped.

sections.body: Each task node holds a description, type, status, execution feedback and dependencies. Each task is expanded into an action graph of code nodes. A stateful graph executor runs the code, lets the LLM debug it for a predefined number of attempts, and flags the task as Failure if the problem persists. For failed tasks, the task graph is regenerated, sorted topologically and compared with the original by prefix matching, so unchanged tasks before the fork are kept. Tool selection ranks candidate tools and keeps the top-k, and it is bypassed when no tool fits. This section gives no quantitative evaluation.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Data Interpreter represents a workflow as a task graph whose tasks expand into action graphs of executable code.

sections.body: Four benchmarks are used. InfiAgent-DABench has 257 challenges from 52 CSV files, scored by accuracy. ML-Benchmark has 8 Kaggle datasets scored by comprehensive score, and the open-ended benchmark has 20 tasks scored by completion rate. MATH uses four categories of level-5 problems. On InfiAgent-DABench, the gpt-4o version improves results by 25% over direct LLM inference. On ML-Benchmark, Data Interpreter scores 0.95 against 0.88 for OpenDevin and 0.86 for AutoGen. In the ablation, iterative graph refinement improved performance by 0.48, and programmable node generation raised the comprehensive score by 10.6% to 0.94. With gpt-4-0613 the agent scored 73.55 and did not beat direct inference, which the authors attribute to context overflow.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Data Interpreter scores 0.95 on ML-Benchmark and 0.97 on open-ended tasks, above every listed baseline.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the approach: hierarchical graph representation with iterative task refinement, fine-grained execution, validation and modification. It states that the framework monitors data changes and adapts to dynamic environments. The authors claim it outperforms various open-source frameworks in machine learning tasks, mathematical problems and real-world applications, and they frame this as an advance for LLM-based data science agents. The conclusion does not restate limits; the appendix covers them.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Hierarchical graph refinement is presented as outperforming open-source frameworks on machine learning, math and real-world tasks.

sections.body:
- **Limits:** the ML datasets are entry-level Kaggle sets under 500MB, mainly classification and regression. Time series, multi-label and multi-table tasks are untested. The agent does not use numerical feedback to refine strategies, so it lacks automatic self-improvement. MATH tests use only level-5 problems because of budget constraints.
- **Broader impact:** tool integration can run malicious code. The authors mitigate this by prompting the agent to check code before generating new code.
- **Details:** Table 5 lists the tools. Open-ended tasks are scored by completion rate. The comprehensive score is an equal-weighted sum of completion rate and normalized performance score.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix states limits: only entry-level Kaggle datasets, no automatic self-improvement, and MATH limited to level-5 problems.
